passages.text: Zongertinib reduces tumor burden in patients. A, Pre- and on-treatment CT scans of a patient having stage IV cholangiocarcinoma (baseline panel) with a SDC4-NRG1 fusion treated with zongertinib and showing a response (day 129 panel). Quantification of the tumor marker CA19-9 in the blood at indicated dates (x-axis; right). B, Pre- and on-treatment CT scans of a patient having stage IV breast cancer (baseline panel) with a HER2V777L exon 20 mutation treated with zongertinib and showing a response at the first evaluation (day 38 panel). Quantification of the tumor marker CA15.3 in the blood at indicated dates (x-axis; right). C, Pre- and on-treatment CT scans of a patient having stage IV breast cancer (baseline panel) with ERBB2 amplification treated with zongertinib and showing a tumor response of the locoregional recurrence (right axilla) at the first evaluation (day 37 panel). No biomarker data are available for this patient.

Together, these three cases demonstrate that zongertinib can induce tumor regressions in heavily pretreated patients suffering from tumors that display relevant HER2 aberrations and that anecdotal clinical activity was also observed beyond NSCLC. The clinical activity of zongertinib was observed in early escalation steps in which patients also received lower doses than the two doses (120 and 240 mg every day) tested for dose optimization.
Discussion

Our data show that zongertinib is a promising treatment option for patients with HER2-dependent cancers. Zongertinib covalently inhibits HER2 with high potency and selectivity across a large panel of kinases, including EGFRWT. In cell proliferation assays, zongertinib potently inhibits the proliferation of not only Ba/F3 cell models dependent on HER2WT or on various HER2 mutants but also human cancer cell lines dependent on HER2, including those expressing NRG1 fusions, HER2YVMA and other mutations, and high levels of HER2WT. Of note, much higher concentrations of zongertinib are required to inhibit the proliferation of Ba/F3 cell models and human cancer cell lines not dependent on HER2, including those dependent on EGFRWT. The sensitivity of a large panel of human cancer cell lines toward zongertinib correlates with HER2WT expression levels. These results demonstrate that selective pharmacological inhibition of HER2 mirrors the results of genetic inhibition of HER2, observed in large-scale CRISPR-Cas9 and RNAi screens. In vivo, single-agent zongertinib treatment inhibits the growth and reduces the size of tumors in cell line-derived (HER2WT-high expression or HER2YVMA-dependent) and PDX (HER2YVMA dependent) models.

Consistent with in vitro biochemical assay results and cell proliferation results, zongertinib treatment time- and dose-dependently downregulates phosphorylated HER2, as well as downstream MAPK and PI3K signaling pathways, in cells dependent on HER2. Zongertinib treatment reduces not only the level of phosphorylated ERK but also the expression of ERK target genes, such as DUSP6, SPRY4, ETV4, ETV5, and FOSL1. Consistent with the selectivity of zongertinib in biochemical assays in inhibiting HER2 over EGFRWT, considerably higher doses are required to reduce EGFR phosphorylation levels in an EGFRWT-dependent cell line.

Zongertinib binds the ATP-binding site of HER2 and forms a covalent bond with cysteine 805. As demonstrated in this study, this covalent binding of HER2 is critical for the high potency of zongertinib in inhibiting cell proliferation. This mechanism of action of zongertinib is clearly different from that of T-DM1 and T-DXd. Although both ADCs rely on trastuzumab to bind to HER2-expressing cells, they differ in the attached cytotoxic moiety. T-DM1 utilizes a microtubule inhibitor, whereas T-DXd utilizes a topoisomerase I inhibitor. Using a cell line model, we demonstrate that zongertinib combines well with HER2-directed ADCs and potently inhibits the proliferation of HER2-dependent cells that have acquired resistance to T-DXd. In a HER2-dependent xenograft model, we show that adding zongertinib enhances the antitumor activity of T-DXd and T-DM1. The data presented in this study raise the exciting possibility that zongertinib may be effective in treating HER2-dependent tumors that are resistant to these ADCs and indicate that adding zongertinib may expand the population of patients who would benefit from HER2-targeting ADCs.

A recent exciting development in the treatment of patients with NSCLC is the approval of KRASG12C inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib to treat patients whose tumors express KRASG12C, which account for about 13% of NSCLC cases. KRAS is a major downstream mediator of ERBB signaling. Preclinical studies have shown that cotargeting an oncogenic KRAS mutant with EGFR more potently inhibits cells dependent on that KRAS mutant than targeting the KRAS mutant alone, leaving room to speculate if selective inhibition of other ERBB members would result in a synergistic combination effect. We demonstrate in this study that zongertinib inhibits the growth of a KRASG12C-dependent xenograft model synergistically with both sotorasib and adagrasib and that a combination of zongertinib with adagrasib induces persistent tumor shrinkage in a PDX model, whereas neither alone can induce this effect.

Our clinical data confirm the preclinical hypothesis that selective HER2 inhibition while sparing EGFRWT can permit doses in patients, with evidence of activity in patients with tumors with aberrant HER2 activation, either through expression of a ligand fusion reported to signal through HER2 or expression of an oncogenic HER2 mutant or aberrantly high levels of HER2. A manuscript describing the clinical results of a dose expansion clinical trial is currently in preparation for publication.

In summary, our study indicates that zongertinib is a promising treatment option for patients with HER2-dependent solid cancers as monotherapy and as concurrent treatment with ADC therapy or with KRAS-targeted drugs.
Methods
Synthesis of Zongertinib (N-(1-(8-((3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)phenyl)amino)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidin-2-yl)piperidin-4-yl)acrylamide)
An overview of the synthetic routes to zongertinib and BI-3999 is shown in Supplementary Fig. S1, and graphical NMR spectra are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2.

3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)aniline (500 mg, 1.97 mmol) and 8-chloro-2-(methylthio)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidine hydrochloride (492 mg, 1.97 mmol) were suspended in isopropanol, and the resulting reaction mixture stirred at 50 C for 3 hours, at which time high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS) indicated full conversion. The reaction mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure, and the crude product was redissolved in dichloromethane and washed with aqueous NaHCO3. The organic layer was dried over Na2SO4 and concentrated, and the resulting crude product was purified by column chromatography (SiO2, gradient of 0%-15% methanol in dichloromethane) to afford the product (840 mg).

N-(3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)phenyl)-6-(methylthio)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidin-4-amine (860 mg, 90%, 1.80 mmol) was suspended in dichloromethane (30 mL), and the resulting mixture was cooled to 0 C to 5 C. mCPBA (3-chloroperbenzoic acid, 444 mg, 77%, 1.98 mmol) was added portionwise over 1 hour, and the resulting reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature overnight, at which time HPLC-MS indicated full conversion. The reaction mixture was diluted with dichloromethane and washed with aqueous NaHCO3. The organic layer was dried over Na2SO4 and concentrated, and the resulting crude product which was used directly in the next step (767 mg, crude).

N-(3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)phenyl)-6-(methylsulfinyl)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidin-4-amine (5.42 g, 80%, 9.73 mmol) was dissolved in N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF, 50 mL) and diisopropylethylamine (2.8 mL, 16 mmol). 4-Boc-amino-1-piperidine (2.39 g, 11.9 mmol) was added, and the reaction was stirred at 60 C overnight. Then, the reaction mixture was concentrated, and the crude product was used directly in the next step (5.66 g, crude).

Tert-butyl (1-(8-((3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)phenyl)amino)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidin-2-yl)piperidin-4-yl)carbamate (5.66 g, 9.73 mmol) was dissolved in dichloromethane (100 mL) and methanol (30 mL). Four mol/L HCl in dioxane (11 mL, 44 mmol) was added, and the resulting reaction mixture was heated to 45 C for 7 hours. HPLC-MS indicated some remaining starting material; therefore, the reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature overnight. Four mol/L HCl in dioxane (1 mL, 0.40 mmol) was added, and the reaction mixture was reheated to 45 C for 4 hours, at which time HPLC-MS indicated full conversion. The reaction mixture was concentrated, and the resulting crude product was purified by column chromatography (SiO2, gradient of 0%-20% methanol in dichloromethane) to afford the product (4.5 g, 70% purity).

1-[8-({3-methyl-4-[(1-methyl-1H-1,3-benzodiazol-5-yl)oxy]phenyl}amino)-[1,3]diazino[5,4-d]pyrimidin-2-yl]piperidin-4-amine (4.5 g, 70%, 6.9 mmol) was suspended in dichloromethane (150 mL) and triethyl amine (4 mL, 28 mmol), and dimethylaminopyridine (115 mg, 0.941 mmol) was added. Then, acroyloyl anhydride (1.36 g, 95%, 10.3 mmol) was added, and the resulting reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 1 hour, at which time HPLC-MS indicated full conversion. The reaction mixture was diluted with dichloromethane (50 mL) and washed with aqueous NaHCO3 and brine. The organic layer was dried over Na2SO4 and concentrated, and the resulting crude product was purified by column chromatography (SiO2, gradient of 0%-20% methanol in dichloromethane) to afford the product (2.49 g).
Synthesis of BI-3999 (N-(1-(8-((3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)phenyl)amino)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidin-2-yl)piperidin-4-yl)acetamide)

6-(4-aminopiperidin-1-yl)-N-(3-methyl-4-((1-methyl-1H-benzo[d]imidazol-5-yl)oxy)phenyl)pyrimido[5,4-d]pyrimidin-4-amine (100 mg, 208 mmol) and 4-dimethylaminopyridine (2.5 mg, 0.02 mmol) were suspended in 5 mL dichloromethane. Acetic anhydride (25 muL, 0.23 mmol) was added, and the resulting reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for one hour. Then, the reaction mixture was diluted with dichloromethane and washed with aqueous NaHCO3 and brine. Then, the layers were separated, and the organic layer was dried over MgSO4 and concentrated. The crude product was purified by column chromatography (SiO2, gradient of 0%-10% methanol in dichloromethane) to afford the product (75 mg).
Kinase Panel

Kinase selectivity was investigated using the Thermo Fisher Scientific SelectScreen kinase profiling services measuring single-point inhibition at 1 mumol/L for a broad panel of kinases and dose-response curves for selected kinases.
Cell Lines

Cell lines used for cell proliferation assays and immunoblots were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) (AU565, BT-474, CFPAC-1, CHL-1, HCC1419, HCC1954, HCC4006, LS513, MDA-MB-175-VII, MDA-MB-453, NCI-H2170, NCI-N87, SK-BR-3, and SW-13), European Collection of Animal Cell Cultures (ECACC) (HT115), Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank (JCRB) (HuH-7, MKN7, and RMG-I), Deutsche Sammlung von Mikroorganismen und Zellkulturen (DSMZ) (MFE-280, OE19, RT-112, and SK-GT-2), Korean Cell Line Bank (KCLB) (SNU-216), or Arterand (SUM190PT) and cultivated according to the suppliers' recommendations, except for MDA-MB-175-VII. All cell lines were Mycoplasma-tested and validated by next-generation sequencing (NGS) and short tandem repeat profiling (STR). Master cell banks were made upon purchasing individual lines, and fresh aliquots were used for the experiments. For proliferation assays and immunoblots shown in Fig. 3C and D, MDA-MB-175-II cells were kept under suppliers' recommendations for all other assays. MDA-MB-175-VII cells were cultivated at 37 C and 5% CO2 in DMEM (Sigma-Aldrich, D4629) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco, 26140079), GlutaMAX (Gibco, 35050038), and sodium pyruvate (Gibco, 11360039). Ba/F3 cell lines were generated as described previously. PC-9 HER2YVMA ARTi cell lines were generated as previously described for the EGFRdel19 variant using a pMSCV-driven HER2YVMA-dsRed-ARTi construct. Knockdown was induced with doxycycline in the drinking water (2 mg/mL with 2% Sucrose). ARTi studies were conducted in NMRI-Foxn1nu mice.
Proliferation Assay

Cells were seeded in white, sterile 96-well or 384-well culture plates (white with white flat bottom, TC-treated; PerkinElmer, #6005680 or #6007680). In general, seeded cells were incubated overnight in a humidified incubator at 37 C and 5% CO2; exceptions were MDA-MB-453 and SW-13, which were grown at 37 C but without CO2. 0.1% DMSO-control or serial compound dilution in triplicates was added. After 5 days of incubation with test compounds, the cells plates were measured upon the addition of CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Reagent (Promega, Cat. No. G9243) to assess cell viability. The plates were placed on a shaker for 5 minutes and additionally incubated for 10 minutes at room temperature to induce cell lysis and to stabilize the luminescent signal. The luminescent signal of each well was measured using an EnSpire or EnSight multilabel plate reader (PerkinElmer). The IC50 values were calculated using Boehringer Ingelheim's proprietary software MegaLab, and curve fitting was based on the program PRISM, GraphPad Inc.
Immunoblots

Logarithmically growing cells were harvested and lysed, 14 mug total protein was loaded per lane, and gels were transferred to PVDF membranes (Bio-Rad, #1704157) after saturation of membranes with 5% milk in TBS-T. The following primary antibodies were added [all antibodies were obtained from Cell Signaling Technology, HER2 (#4290)]: pHER2 [#6942 (p-Y1196) or #2247 (p-Y1248)], HER3 (#12708), HER4 (#4795), pERK (#4370), ERK (#9102), pAKT (#4058), AKT (#9272), and beta-Actin (#4967). Goat anti-rabbit horseradish peroxidase-linked antibody was obtained from Dako (#P0448). Enhanced chemiluminescence signal (using GE Healthcare, #RPN2106, or Merck, #64-202BP) was detected using X-ray films.
Simple Western Capillary Immunoassay

A total of 1 x 105 cells were plated per well in a 24-well plate. The next day, the cells were treated with zongertinib, poziotinib, or T-DXd for 6 hours. The cells were then washed with 1 mL of PBS and lysed with 50 muL with RIPA lysis buffer (R2078, Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with HaltTM proteinase inhibitor cocktail (1:100, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 78438) and 0.25 muL Benzonase nuclease (Millipore, 70746). Four muL of lysate was taken for Western (WES) analysis using 12 to 230 kDa Separation Module (ProteinSimple, SM-W004). The following antibodies were used: HER2 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 4290), pHER2-Tyr1196 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 6942), EGFR (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 4267), pEGFR- Tyr1068 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 3777), ERK 1/2 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 9102), pERK 1/2 -Thr202/Tyr204 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 4370), AKT (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 9272), pAKT-Ser473 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 4060), DUSP6 (1:100, Abcam, ab76310), S6 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 2217), pS6 -Ser235/236 (1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 2211), and GAPDH (1:300, Abcam, ab9485). WES data were analyzed using Compass for SW software (v6.1.0, ProteinSimple).
Phosphoprotein In Vivo Biomarker Analyses

pERK and pHER2 modulations in tumors were determined using the phospho/total ERK1/2 (Meso Scale Diagnostics, K15107D) or phospho (Tyr1248)/total ErbB2 (Meso Scale Diagnostics, K15125D) whole-cell lysate kits, respectively, as recommended by the manufacturer. Briefly, tumors were homogenized in lysis buffer (Meso Scale Discovery, product code R60TX-2) supplemented with 1:100 phosphatase inhibitor cocktail #2 (Sigma-Aldrich, product code P5726), phosphatase inhibitor cocktail #3 (Sigma-Aldrich, product code P0044), protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, product code 11836170001), 1 mmol/L phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (Sigma-Aldrich, product code P7626), and 0.1% SDS (Sigma-Aldrich, product code 75746) using ReadyPrep mini grinders (Bio-Rad, product code 163-2146) and resin tubes (Bio-Rad, product code 163-2146) as recommended by the manufacturer. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation (10 minutes, 10,000 x g) and analyzed using a MESO SECTOR S 600 reader (Meso Scale Discovery).
Gene Expression In Vivo Biomarker Analyses

For DUSP6 modulation in tumors, RNA was isolated using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, product code 73404). Less than 50 mg tumor (typically around 10 mg) was homogenized in 900 muL QIAzol lysis reagent using a TissueLyser II device (Qiagen, 1 minute, 30 Hz), adding a 5-mm stainless steel bead per tube. All further steps of RNA purification were carried out as specified by the manufacturer using 1-bromo-2-chloropropane (Sigma-Aldrich, product code B9673) instead of chloroform. RNA samples were analyzed using QuantiGene Singleplex Assay Kit (Invitrogen, product code QS0013) and Singleplex RNA probes (Invitrogen, product code QGS-200; assay IDs SA-11958 for DUSP6 and SA-10057 for TBP as a houskeeping gene). Alternatively, RNA was analyzed by reverse transcription and sequencing as detailed below.
Solubility

Solubility measurement of zongertinib was conducted using the shake flask method. Samples up to a compound concentration of ~1 mg/mL were shaken in the respective solvent for 2 hours at room temperature. After filtrating the samples, the compound concentration in the filtrate was determined using HPLC-UV.
Determination of Bidirectional Permeability in MDCK-MDR1 and MDCK-BCRP Cells

Assessment of bidirectional permeability was conducted as described previously using MDCK-MDR1 and MCKD-BCRP cells instead of Caco-2 cells. Briefly, after reconstitution in culture media, assay-ready frozen cells were seeded onto Transwell inserts (#3379, Corning). The cells were cultured at 37 C and 95% relative humidity in the presence of 5% CO2 for 9 to 10 days. For permeability assessment, the compounds were diluted in transport buffer (128.13 mmol/L NaCl, 5.36 mmol/L KCl, 1 mmol/L MgSO4, 1.8 mmol/L CaCl2, 4.17 mmol/L NaHCO3, 1.19 mmol/L Na2HPO4, 0.41 mmol/L NaH2PO4, 15 mmol/L 2-[4-(2-hydroxyethyl)piperazin-1-yl]ethanesulfonic acid, 20 mmol/L glucose, pH 7.4, and 0.25% BSA) at a final compound concentration of 10 mumol/L. The incubation solution was added to the apical or basal donor compartment, and transport buffer without test compounds was added to the opposite receiver compartment and incubated for up to 2 hours. Samples were taken at different time points, followed by test compound concentration quantification by LC-MS/MS. Apparent permeability coefficients (Papp,AB, Papp,BA) were calculated as follows:in which Q is defined as the amount of compound recovered in the receiver compartment after the incubation time t, C0 as the initial compound concentration given to the donor compartment, and s as the surface area of the Transwell inserts. The efflux ratio is calculated as the quotient of Papp,BA to Papp,AB (each mean of duplicates). In both cell types, one reference compound (apafant in MDCK-MDR1 and daizein for MDCK-BCRP) as well as a low-permeable compound (BI internal reference, Papp   3 x 10-7 cm/seconds, no efflux) were included as assay controls. The different references, as well as transepithelial electrical resistance measurements before the permeability assay, were used to ensure the quality of the assays.
Assessment of Plasma Protein Binding In Vitro

Binding of research compounds to plasma protein was determined using the equilibrium dialysis method, as described previously. Briefly, plasma of different species was spiked with 3 mumol/L (1% v/v DMSO) of the test compound and dialyzed in equilibrium dialysis cells (RED-device, Thermo Fisher Scientific) against 100 mmol/L potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, for up for 5 hours at 37 C through a semipermeable membrane. After the incubation, donor and acceptor compartments were precipitated, and the compound concentrations were determined by HPLC-MS/MS. Calibration and quality control samples were prepared using blank plasma and the internal standard. The fraction unbound (fu) is calculated as the ratio of the compound concentration in the acceptor compartment to the concentration in the donor compartment using technical triplicates.
Assessment of Metabolic Stability in Hepatocytes In Vitro

The metabolic stability kinetics of the test compound was assessed in a hepatocyte suspension assay. Briefly, 1 mumol/L test compound (at a final DMSO concentration of 0.05% v/v) was incubated in the presence of 1 Mio cells/mL at 37 C and 5% CO2 in a humidified incubator. Samples were taken at six different time points up to 4 hours. Reactions were terminated by the addition of acetonitrile, and precipitates were separated by centrifugation. The compound concentration in supernatants was determined by HPLC-MS/MS, and clearance was calculated from compound half-lives using the well-stirred liver model. In each species incubation, two different references (one low- and one high-stability reference), as well as a cell-free chemical stability quality control, were included and used to ensure the quality of the assays.
Prediction of Human PK and Therapeutic Dose
PK data (i.v. and oral administration) determined in mouse, rat, dog, and minipig models were used to predict human PK properties of zongertinib (see Supplementary Fig. S1B).

Human clearance was predicted based on the in vitro/in vivo correlation using in vitro hepatocyte data and in vivo clearance data after i.v. administration, according to the following equation:in which Cl is the total body plasma clearance in human, Clin vivo,predicted is the predicted hepatic metabolic blood clearance from in vitro data, and a and b are the parameters obtained from the regression analysis of the clearance values across multiple species.
Human Vss was predicted based on the mean of the measured animal Vss values corrected for species-dependent plasma-protein binding.

Oral bioavailability (F) was calculated using the average of the measured animal data. The absorption rate constant (ka) was predicted as the mean ka values from mouse, rat, dog, and minipig models. The ka values of the different species were determined by fitting the animal data to a one-compartment PK model with first-order oral absorption, no lag time, and first-order elimination.

The predicted human dose for zongertinib was derived from a quantitative PK/TGI model. This preclinical semi-mechanistic mathematical model was built using input data from in vitro assessment as well as in vivo data from the PC-9 HER2YVMA xenograft efficacy experiments. Compound plasma exposure and respective TGI data generated in mice were used to train the quantitative model. The PK/TGI model has consistently and reliably predicted tumor growth kinetics in the PC-9 HER2YVMA xenograft models upon treatment with zongertinib. The PK/TGI model was used to identify the required dose administered in mouse to achieve tumor regressions in the PC-9 HER2YVMA xenograft model. Likewise, the human PK plasma profile of zongertinib was simulated as a one-compartmental PK model using the predicted human PK parameters. Predicted exposures have been further incorporated into the PK/TGI model to estimate the required dose required to achieve a TGI >100% in both every day as well as twice a day dosing regimens.
NGS Library Preparation and Sequencing for Gene Expression Profiling

Cell derived RNA samples were normalized to 100 ng/muL in 10 muL nuclease-free H2O. A measure of 500 ng of total RNA was used as the contribution for genome-wide gene expression profiling by 3' mRNA sequencing. NGS libraries were prepared using QuantSeq 3'mRNA-Seq V2 Library Prep Kit FWD for Illumina (Lexogen GmbH) according to the manufacturer's protocol using the Biomek i7 automated liquid handling workstation (Beckman Coulter GmbH). After quality control by High Sensitivity D1000 ScreenTape on a 4200 TapeStation System (Agilent Technologies Osterreich GmbH), individual libraries were normalized, equimolarly pooled, quantified using NEBNext Library Quant Kit for Illumina (New England BioLabs Inc., #E7630L), and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 or NovaSeq 6000 instrument (Illumina) using 75 bp single-read chemistry.
Gene Expression Profiling (RNA-Seq) and Differential Gene Expression Analysis
See the methods section of.
Clinical Data
Written informed consent was obtained from all patients. Studies were conducted in accordance with recognized ethical guidelines. Studies were approved by an Institutional Review Board.
Real-Word Clinicogenomics Data

Clinicogenomics data from Tempus Labs Inc., coving all major cancer indications, were analyzed to explore overexpression and amplification prevalence across major tumor types. Tempus performed whole-exome RNA-seq, covering ~20,000 genes on clinical formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded material from patients with cancer using a single platform. De-identified clinical and molecular data were analyzed from U.S. pan-cancer patient records. All statistical analyses were performed using R software version (4.2.1). To generate the pan-cancer HER2 overexpression threshold, a logistic regression model was fit to predict ERBB2 diploid or ERBB2 amplified (i.e., >=6 copy number) status using HER2 expression. Using the computed threshold of 7.95 log2 [transcripts per million (TPM + 1)], prevalence of different ERBB2 alterations derived from DNA-seq (amplifications) and RNA-seq (gene expression) were plotted across tumor indications. On independent test data, the expression cutoff for HER2-high obtained a specificity and sensitivity of 0.92. For further details and data, see Supplementary Table S3.
In Vivo Experiments

For the cell line-based xenograft models, mice were group-housed (8-10 mice per cage) under pathogen-free and controlled environmental conditions (21 C +- 1.5 C temperature and 55% +- 10% humidity; 12-hour light-dark cycle) and handled according to the internal institutional, governmental, and European Union guidelines (Austrian Animal Protection Law, ETS-123). Animal studies were approved by the internal Ethics Committee and the local governmental committee. At 6 to 10 weeks old, female NMRI-Foxn1nu mice (Taconic) were engrafted subcutaneously with 2.5 x 106 NCI-N87 cells, 5 x 106 PC-9 EGFRKO,HER2YVMA cells, or 5 x 106 NCI-H2122 cells, respectively.

For PDX models, mice were group-housed under pathogen-free and controlled environmental conditions (20 C-23 C temperature and 30%-70% humidity) and handled according to institutional guidelines. Animal studies were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees. At 6 to 8 weeks old, female athymic Nude-Foxn1nu (Envigo or Charles River Laboratories) were subcutaneously implanted with CTG-2534 or ST524 tumor fragments.

Tumor volumes were measured 2 to 3 times weekly using a caliper. Animals were weighed and examined daily and sacrificed based on severity criteria, including body weight, tumor size, and tumor necrosis. A maximum tumor size of 1,500 mm3 was approved by the Ethics Committee for all models. Mice were sacrificed in case tumor volumes exceeded the limit between measurements. Data collection was performed blind to the condition of the experiments as compound codes were used. Data analysis was not performed blind to the condition of the experiment.
Activity Screen of Zongertinib across HER2 Mutations
This method was previously published and adapted to HER2:
Cell Lines and Culture Conditions

Ba/F3 cells were maintained in RPMI1640 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FBS, 2 mmol/L glutamine, 1% each of penicillin and streptomycin, and mouse IL3 (20 U/mL; Merck). The cells were used for the experiments within 10 passages from thawing. Cell line authentication and Mycoplasma testing were not carried out within 6 months.
MANO Method

A retroviral vector (pcx6-bleo) is utilized to enable stable integration of individual variants into the genome of the Ba/F3 cells along with the 10 bp barcode sequences upstream of the start codon of selected genes. Three clones with individual barcodes were constructed to obtain triplicate data for each assay (Azenta Life Sciences). The plasmids were transduced with packaging plasmids (Takara Bio) into HEK293T cells to produce recombinant retroviral particles. Ba/F3 cells were seeded on RetroNectin-coated (Takara Bio) plates and infected with retroviruses in a medium supplemented with 20 U/mL of IL-3. Ba/F3 cells expressing each variant were mixed in equal amounts and treated with the indicated concentrations of BI31 (100 pmol/L-10 mumol/L or 10% DMSO) as the vehicle control. The experiments were conducted in biological triplicate. At the end of the drug treatment, genomic DNA was extracted from the cell lysates using QIAmp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen), and PCR amplification was performed using NEBNext Q5 Hor Start HiFi PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer's instructions and the primers shown in Supplementary Table S1. The amplicons were purified on AMPure beads (Beckman Coulter). Quality check of the libraries was assessed using a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and the Agilent 2200 TapeStation System (Agilent). The libraries were then sequenced using an Illumina MiSeq system and Reagent Kit V2 (300 cycles), and 150 bp paired-end reads were created (the sequencing primer loaded into the MiSeq cartridge is described in Supplementary Table S1). The barcode sequences 5'-CTAGACTGCCNNNNNNNNNNGGATCACTCT-3' (in which N denotes any nucleotide) were included in the sequencing results, and the number of each barcode in each mutant was quantified. The number of barcodes was used to calculate the cell viability of cells with the variants (Supplementary Table S1). Considering the different doubling times of the integrated cells, DMSO-treated cell mixtures were used as the reference control for normalizing each cell clone signal. The relative growth inhibition of each cell clone was calculated as 100 x (average read number across triplicates)/(average read number of the DMSO control). Variants with fewer than 100 barcode sequence reads were excluded from the analysis. The dose-response curves were fit to the observed cell viabilities using the drc package in R language. The two-parameter log-logistic function LL.2 was used with the following settings: upper (relative viability without drug) = 1, robust = "mean", and method = "Nelder-Mead". The IC50 value was defined as the inflection point on a dose-response curve.
Statistics and Reproducibility

For in vivo experiments, animals per group were determined using power analysis. Power analysis was performed for in vivo studies with a two-sided test, alpha = 0.05 and power 0.80. Animals were randomized according to tumor size at 69 to 303 mm3, tumor volume for cell line-derived models, or at 125 to 311 mm3 tumor volume for CTG-2543 and 78 to 226 mm3 for ST524 after fragment implantation (n = 8-10 per group). No datapoints were excluded from visualization and/or analysis.
PRISM Cell Line Viability Assay

PRISM is a high-throughput multiplexed cancer cell line viability screening platform developed by the Broad Institute of Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard. Zongertinib and BI-1622 were tested in the PRISM assay on 931 cell lines at eight-point dose dilutions (3-fold step dilutions) with a treatment duration of 5 days. Note, that this collection of cell lines does not cover all HER2 oncogenic mechanisms (e.g., mutations). Zongertinib produced AUCs and quality-passing 844 cell lines (713 cell lines excluding hematopoietic and fibroblasts), whereas BI-1622 produced data for 882 cell lines (741 cell lines excluding hematopoietic and fibroblasts). The minimum and maximum doses were set at 0.002286 and 5 mumol/L, respectively. HER2-high TPM values in analysis and visualizations were set to TPM 250 based on the logistic regression model in patient data to compute HER2 overexpression; this cutoff does not inform patient selection or stratification. Data processing from raw intensity values to computed AUC values for each dose-response curve is described in the Supplementary Methods. The analysis code is publicly available on the code repository GitHub (https://github.com/cmap/dockerized_mts). For further details and data, see Supplementary Table S2.
PRISM Methods

The current PRISM cell set consists of 931 cell lines representing more than 45 lineages, including both adherent and suspension/hematopoietic cell lines. These cell lines largely overlap with and reflect the diversity of the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia cell lines (see https://portals.broadinstitute.org/ccle). Cell lines were grown in RPMI 10% FBS without phenol red for adherent lines and RPMI 20% FBS without phenol red for suspension lines. Parental cell lines were stably infected with a unique 24-nucleotide DNA barcode via lentiviral transduction and blasticidin selection. After selection, barcoded cell lines were expanded and QCed (Mycoplasma contamination test, a single-nucleotide polymorphism test for confirming cell line identity, and barcode ID confirmation). Passing barcoded lines were then pooled (20-25 cell lines per pool) based on doubling time and frozen in assay-ready vials. Test compounds were added to 384-well plates and run at 8-point doses with 3-fold dilutions in triplicate. These assay ready plates were then seeded with the thawed cell line pools. Adherent cell pools were plated at 1,250 cells per well, whereas suspension and mixed adherent/suspension pools were plated at 2,000 cells per well. Treated cells were incubated for 5 days and then lysed. Lysate plates were collapsed together prior to barcode amplification and detection.
PRISM Barcode Amplification and Detection

Each cell line's unique barcode is located at the end of the blasticidin resistance gene and gets expressed as mRNA. These mRNAs were captured using magnetic particles that recognize polyA sequences. Captured mRNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA, and then the sequence containing the unique PRISM barcode was amplified by PCR. Finally, Luminex beads that recognize the specific barcode sequences in the cell set were hybridized to the PCR products and detected using a Luminex scanner which reports signal as a median fluorescence intensity (MFI).
PRISM Data Processing
For each plate, we first normalized the logMFI (log2 MFI) of the DMSO wells to their median logMFI.

Each detection well contained 10 control barcodes in increasing abundances as spike-in controls. A monotonic smooth p-spline was fit for each control barcode detection well to normalize the abundance of each barcode to the corresponding value in the plate-wise median DMSO profiles. Next, all the logMFI values in the well were transformed through the inferred spline function to correct for amplification and detection artifacts.

Next, the separability between negative and positive control treatments was assessed. In particular, we used the error rate of the optimum simple threshold classifier between the control samples for each cell line and plate combination. Error rate is a measure of overlap of the two control sets and is defined asin which FP is false positive, FN is false negative, and n is the total number of controls. A threshold was set between the distributions of positive and negative control logMFI values (with everything below the threshold said to be positive and above said to be negative) such that this value is minimized. Additionally, we also filtered based on the dynamic range of each cell line. The dynamic range was defined as in which mu+/- stood for the median of the normalized logMFI values in positive/negative control samples.

We filtered out cell lines with error rates above 0.05 and a dynamic range less than 1.74 from the downstream analysis. Additionally, any cell line that had less than two passing replicates was also omitted for the sake of reproducibility. Finally, we computed viability by normalizing with respect to the median negative control for each plate. Log-fold change viabilities were computed asin which log2 (x) is the corrected logMFI value in the treatment and log2 (mu-) is the median corrected logMFI in the negative control wells in the same plate.
Log-viability scores were corrected for batch effects coming from pools and culture conditions using the ComBat algorithm, as previously described.

passages.text: Alcohol and fear conditioning produce strain-specific changes in the dorsal hippocampal transcriptome of adolescent C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice
Background:

Adolescent sensitivity to alcohol is influenced by genetic background. Data from our laboratory suggested that adolescent C57BL/6J and DBA/2J inbred mice differed in susceptibility to alcohol-induced deficits in dorsal hippocampus-dependent contextual fear learning.
Methods:

To investigate the biological underpinnings of this strain difference, we examined dorsal hippocampus gene expression using RNA-sequencing after alcohol or saline administration followed by Pavlovian fear conditioning across male and female C57BL/6J and DBA/2J adolescents.
Results:

Strains exhibited dramatic differences in dorsal hippocampus gene expression. Specifically, C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains differed by 3526 transcripts in males and 2675 transcripts in females. We identified pathways likely to be involved in mediating alcohol's effects on learning, including networks associated with Chrna7, a gene encoding the nicotinic cholinergic receptor alpha 7 subunit, and Fmr1, a gene encoding the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein.
Conclusions:

These findings provide insight into the mechanisms underlying strain differences in alcohol's effects on learning and suggest that different biological networks are recruited for learning based on genetics, sex, and alcohol exposure.
INTRODUCTION

Understanding the basic mechanisms of individual sensitivity to alcohol is an important step in addressing the global health problem of Alcohol Use Disorders (AUD). The path to alcohol dependence or addiction starts with an individual's first experience with alcohol, which usually occurs during adolescence. Whether this first experience is positive or negative can predict the trajectory of lifetime alcohol use. Genetics can shape sensitivity to numerous consequences of alcohol, including reports of subjective intoxication  and hangover. Preclinical research indicates that genetic background can determine alcohol-related behavioral phenotypes, such as conditioned taste aversion (CTA) in adult and adolescent male mice. However, little is known about the genetic factors that mediate alcohol's effects on learning and memory in adolescents.

Prior studies from our laboratory found that adult and adolescent male and female C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice were differentially affected by acute alcohol exposure prior to fear conditioning. DBA/2J mice were less susceptible to alcohol-induced contextual, but not cued, fear conditioning deficits than C57BL/6J mice. Because this strain difference was specific to contextual fear learning, this result suggested that the neural circuitry unique to the contextual learning task was differentially affected by alcohol exposure. The dorsal hippocampus is known to be uniquely involved in contextual, but not cued, fear conditioning. Further, hippocampal gene expression varies across inbred mouse strains, which could contribute to differences in learning and sensitivity to disruption of learning. Alcohol exposure and learning both cause changes in hippocampal gene expression. Learning leads to the expression of immediate early genes and a later phase of gene expression changes. It has also been shown that alcohol induces differential changes in hippocampal gene expression between males of C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mouse strains. Therefore, we reasoned that alcohol's effects on dorsal hippocampus gene expression might differ by strain, which could contribute to differences in susceptibility to alcohol's effects on contextual fear learning.

To test this prediction, male and female C57BL/6J and DBA/2J subjects underwent alcohol or saline treatment and fear conditioning or no conditioning (learning or no-learning) control conditions prior to dorsal hippocampus gene expression analysis. RNA-sequencing was chosen for unbiased identification of neurobiological factors altered in a strain-specific manner by alcohol. Based on prior reports, we expected pathway analysis to reveal alcohol-induced changes in neural gene expression broadly related to neuroplasticity. Prior studies in male rats investigating adult hippocampal gene expression after prior adolescent alcohol exposure identified changes related to neurogenesis, long-term potentiation, and myelination. We predicted that we could see similar dysregulated gene networks in adolescent mice, as well as adolescent-specific effects. We have observed sex differences in learning performance after alcohol exposure in C57BL/6J and DBA/2J adolescent and adult mice . Sex differences in gene expression patterns induced by contextual learning or alcohol exposure have been reported in other studies. Because of this, we also expected to see sex-specific gene expression patterns.

The following research examines how genetic background influences changes in gene expression pathways in the dorsal hippocampus after adolescent alcohol exposure, which may contribute to the predisposition or protection for individual cognitive effects of acute alcohol exposure during adolescence. Ultimately, the identification of genes and neurobiological networks associated with alcohol-induced changes in cognition may aid in the development of treatments and interventions for those experiencing alcohol-related learning deficits.
METHODS
Subjects

Subjects were male and female C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice shipped in groups of four from The Jackson laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA; JAX). Mice arrived at the facility on PND 31 (+-3) and were PND 38 (+-3) at the beginning of fear conditioning. This adolescent age was chosen because of important developmental processes happening around this time and based on our prior study examining alcohol effects on fear conditioning in adolescent mice. Subjects were housed in groups of four, and each subject within a cage was allocated to a different treatment group from its cage mates. Final group sizes were 3-4 per sex per strain per treatment group. Mice were kept on a 12-h light/dark cycle (lights on at 7 a.m.) and given free access to food (LabDiet 5053, Lab Diet, St Louis, MO, USA) and water. All procedures occurred between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., during the light phase. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. All procedures were also approved by the Penn State Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
Alcohol dose and route of administration

Mice were administered an acute intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of 0.9% saline solution or 1.5 g/kg 20% w/v ethanol in 0.9% saline solution. The route of administration, dose, and concentration of alcohol were chosen to match our previous studies examining alcohol effects on learning in adolescent C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice. In our previous work, this alcohol dose did not produce strain or sex differences in blood ethanol concentration. A reduction in freezing during the baseline (pre-training) phase of fear conditioning was observed . However, learning deficits were exhibited during contextual fear testing, which happened the day after training and alcohol administration. Thus, locomotor stimulation due to acute alcohol treatment would not have been present during the assessment of contextual learning.
Fear conditioning procedures

Fear conditioning training was conducted by our laboratory as it has been done previously. Fans provided a 65 dB background noise in the room. Mice were placed into sound-attenuating chambers (18.8 x 20 x 18.3 cm; MED Associates, St Albans, VT, USA), and after 2 min, subjects were exposed to two CS-US pairings (CS: Conditioned Stimulus, tone, 30 s, 85 dB; US: Unconditioned Stimulus, 0.45 mA footshock) separated by 120 s. At the conclusion of training, subjects were removed from the training context and moved back to their cages. While an auditory cue was presented during training in order to replicate procedures from our prior work in which an auditory CS was present , the goal of the described experiments was to determine gene expression patterns associated with alcohol's effects on a brain region critical for contextual fear learning:the dorsal hippocampus, and not cued fear learning. This is because the prior studies found greater deficits in contextual fear conditioning. Learning-associated freezing responses to this fear conditioning paradigm are similar between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains independent of alcohol exposure. However, strain differences in other fear conditioning behaviors have been noted.
Experimental timeline

On approximately PND 38, male and female C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice were injected with saline or alcohol. Fifteen minutes later, mice in the learning groups were placed into conditioning chambers and underwent fear conditioning training. Thirty minutes after being removed from the fear conditioning chambers, subjects in the learning groups were euthanized via cervical dislocation. Subjects in the no-learning groups remained in their cages for 50 min and 30 s after saline or alcohol treatment before being euthanized. The no-learning groups had a 50 min and 30 s delay between treatment and tissue collection to mirror the 15 min period after saline or alcohol treatment, the 5 min and 30 s conditioning period, and the 30 min delay after fear conditioning experienced by the learning groups (see Figure 1 for timeline). Subjects in the learning and no-learning groups were kept in the same holding room prior to tissue collection. Sample collection was run across 2 days and groups were counterbalanced to account for potential circadian effects. No-learning control subjects were kept in their cages and not introduced to the training context because the goal of the study was to understand alcohol's effects on contextual fear learning and we wanted to capture gene expression changes that were independent of a new context in our control group.

Contextual fear learning induces at least two waves of transcription and protein synthesis in the hippocampus. During the first wave of transcription, the largest change in gene expression has been observed 30 min after fear conditioning in rodents. Other studies in adult subjects have found significant fear conditioning-induced gene expression changes at this timepoint, including studies in adolescent subjects. Our laboratory has also examined neurobiological markers at this timepoint, finding increased hippocampal CREB phosphorylation 30 min after fear conditioning in acute nicotine-treated adult mice. Thus, we chose the 30 min post-fear conditioning training timepoint for our examination of alcohol's effects on learning-related gene expression.
Tissue collection, RNA isolation, and RNA-sequencing

After euthanasia, the whole hippocampus was dissected, and the dorsal hippocampus was removed and placed in RNAlater (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA). Samples were stored at 4 C for 48 h before being dry-blotted and stored at -80 C until later processing. Trizol and Qiagen RNeasy Kits (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA) were used to extract RNA. Library preparation and sequencing was performed by the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences Genomics Core Facility (RRID:SCR_023645). Uniquely dual indexed libraries were prepared using the Illumina Stranded mRNA Prep Kit (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). Illumina NextSeq 550 High Output 75 nt single read sequencing was performed (Illumina).
RNA-sequencing data analysis

The Penn State Bioinformatics Consulting Center oversaw RNA-sequencing data analysis for this project. Using HISAT2 (v2.1), FASTQ files were aligned to a mouse reference genome (GRCm38). Read counts and differential expression analysis were performed using Salmon (v1.4) or featureCounts (v2.0.1) and DESeq2 (v4.1.1), using a standard FDR cut-off of 0.05. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA; run May 2022; www.qiagen.com/ingenuity; Qiagen, Redwood City, CA, USA) and Enrichr Gene Ontology (GO) analysis were used to interpret data, as our laboratory has done previously. The IPA analysis specified pathways in mammalian nervous tissue or cell lines and the maximum was set to 35 molecules per network. Gene ontology plots were generated using GeneScape. Male and female subjects were analyzed separately due to sex differences in prior behavioral data and apparent sex-specific changes in gene expression. RNA-seq data were uploaded to Gene Expression Omnibus.
qPCR

Reverse transcription was performed with ~1 mug total RNA using the High-Capacity RNA to cDNA kit (ThermoFisher Scientific Applied Biosystems: USA; catalog # 4387406) following manufacturers' instructions. Relative expression was conducted using a TaqMan Universal Mastermix II with UNG (ThermoFisher Scientific Applied Biosystems: USA; catalog # 4440038) to amplify Taqman inventoried primers for Chrna7 (Mm01312230_m1; ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) and Fmr1 (Mm01339582_m1; ThermoFisher Scientific, USA). ThermoFisher Scientific (Life Technologies, USA) custom made primers for Hprt1 (forward: GCTGGTGAAAAGGACCTCT and reverse: CACAGGACTAGAACACCTGC) were used as an endogenous control for each real time quantitative PCR (qPCR) assay. Samples were run in triplicate and averaged with the comparative Ct method to calculate fold change. All amplifications were performed using a Rotor-Gene Q 5 plex HRM thermocycler (Qiagen). Statistical analysis [4-way (strain, sex, drug, and learning condition) ANOVA] was conducted using SPSS 26 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) and figures were made in GraphPad Prism 9 (San Diego, CA, USA).
SNP analysis
Follow-up SNP analysis of genes of interest was conducted using a Mouse Phenome Database GenomeMUSter tool (; https://mpd.jax.org/genotypes).
RESULTS
Overlap of transcripts between alcohol and learning treatment groups

First, the transcripts regulated by alcohol, learning, and combined alcohol and learning exposures (Tables S1-S12) were compared within-strain and within-sex groups. Across males and females from C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains, alcohol exposure led to 114-142 differentially regulated transcripts and fear conditioning led to 128-279 differentially regulated transcripts. Combined alcohol and learning led to 116-473 differentially regulated transcripts. Relatively few transcripts (3-7) were changed across all three conditions (Figure 2).
Individual impact of strain, alcohol, and learning on gene expression
Strain differences in gene expression

Separate pairwise comparisons were conducted to investigate the unique impacts of strain, alcohol exposure, and learning on dorsal hippocampal gene expression patterns. First, the influence of strain was assessed by comparing saline-treated C57BL/6J and DBA/2J that had not undergone fear conditioning (saline no-learning C57BL/6J vs. saline no-learning DBA/2J; Tables S13 and S14). Transcript analysis identified extensive strain differences, finding 3526 transcripts in males and 2675 transcripts in females that were significantly different between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains (FDR <0.05). A notable differentially regulated transcript between strains among male subjects was Chrna7, which encodes the nicotinic cholinergic receptor alpha 7 subunit and has previously been associated with alcohol-induced contextual learning outcomes . IPA analysis identified a significant differentially regulated network associated with this transcript, described as functioning in "Cancer, Organismal Injury and Abnormalities, and Organismal Survival" (score = 27, Figure 3). Follow-up analysis of Chrna7 sequence in C57BL/6J versus DBA/2J strains using a Mouse Phenome Database GenomeMUSter tool revealed mainly intronic, synonymous, or UTR SNPs (Table S15). Follow-up qPCR analysis recapitulated strain differences in Chrna7 expression, although they were not significant (p > 0.05) likely due to low power due to small sample sizes (Figure S1). These results in untreated/untrained male strains implicate predisposing genes and networks that may influence subsequent susceptibility to alcohol deficits in learning.
Impact of alcohol or learning on gene expression

Next, comparisons within strain and sex groups assessed the impact of alcohol and learning on dorsal hippocampal transcript levels. As mentioned previously, alcohol exposure led to 134 (C57BL/6J male), 142 (C57BL/6J female), 141 (DBA/2J male), and 114 (DBA/2J female) differentially regulated transcripts (alcohol no-learning vs. saline no-learning; Tables S1, S4, S7, S10). Fear conditioning resulted in 279 (C57BL/6J male), 133 (C57BL/6J female), 128 (DBA/2J male), and 128 (DBA/2J female) differentially regulated transcripts (saline learning vs. saline no-learning; Tables S2, S5, S8, S11).
Disruption of learning-related gene expression by alcohol

A primary goal of transcriptome analysis of the dorsal hippocampus was to identify the set of fear learning-associated differentially expressed genes that were disrupted by alcohol. This goal was addressed by conducting pairwise comparisons between saline- and alcohol-treated subjects that had undergone fear conditioning training (learning groups only; C57BL/6J alcohol learning vs. C57BL/6J saline learning; Tables S16-S19). Separate analyses were conducted in C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains to assess possibly divergent gene expression patterns associated with disruption of learning by alcohol in both strains. Comparisons between fear conditioned saline- or alcohol-treated C57BL/6J subjects found 176-190 differentially regulated transcripts. Significant GO Biological Pathways were axon regeneration (GO:0031103) and neuron projection regeneration (GO:0031102) in males, while none were significantly enriched in females. IPA analysis identified the following top associated canonical pathways, upstream regulators, and diseases and disorders implicated in transcript-level differences between groups (Tables 1 and 2; Table S20). While top canonical pathways and upstream regulators show pronounced sex differences, diseases and disorders associated with gene expression changes after alcohol were similar across sexes.

Comparisons between fear conditioned saline- or alcohol-treated DBA/2J subjects (DBA/2J alcohol learning vs. DBA/2J saline learning) identified 123-140 differentially regulated transcripts. GO Biological Function analysis did not identify any significantly enriched terms among differentially regulated transcripts in DBA/2J mice. IPA analysis found the listed top five canonical pathways, upstream regulators, and diseases and disorders associated with differentially regulated transcripts (Tables 3 and 4; Table S20). Again, there is only overlap between DBA/2J males and females in diseases and disorders associated with alcohol-regulated transcripts in fear conditioned mice. While there is no overlap in top canonical pathways and upstream regulators between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J analyses, diseases and disorders associated with transcriptional changes were similar between strains.
Strain differences in disruption of learning-related gene expression by alcohol

Another goal of transcriptome analysis was to understand why adolescent DBA/2J mice were less susceptible to alcohol-induced contextual fear learning deficits than C57BL/6J mice in our previous studies. To investigate the individual and combined effects of alcohol, learning, and strain on gene expression, two sets of multifactor (2 x 2) analyses were conducted. First, within-strain and within-sex groups, drug and learning effects were assessed (saline or alcohol vs. learning or no-learning). Then, within sex groups, strain and combined learning and alcohol effects were compared (C57BL/6J or DBA/2J vs. alcohol and learning or saline and no-learning; Table S21). There were no significant interactions of drug and learning condition or strain and combined learning/drug conditions detected (FDR >0.05), likely due to small sample sizes (n = 3-4) when sexes were analyzed separately. Thus, simpler pairwise analyses were used to assess impacts of alcohol, learning, and strain on gene expression, as has been previously published.

Pairwise comparisons were made between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice that had undergone alcohol treatment and fear conditioning exposure (C57BL/6J alcohol learning vs. DBA/2J alcohol learning; Tables S22 and S23). This analysis identified 2816-3847 differentially regulated transcripts between strains. GO Biological Process analysis found ubiquinone biosynthetic process (GO:0006744), cotranslational protein targeting to membrane (GO:0006613), SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane (GO:0006614), cytoplasmic translation (GO:0002181), quinone biosynthetic process (GO:1901663), and protein targeting to ER (GO:0045047) significantly enriched in males, and regulation of focal adhesion assembly (GO:0051893) and neuron projection development (GO:0031175) was significantly enriched in females. Further, IPA analysis identified the following top canonical pathways, upstream regulators, and diseases and disorders associated with transcript differences (Tables 5 and 6; Table S20). Using GeneScape, the functions of upstream regulator genes (as listed in Table 6) were projected to be broadly involved in protein binding and protein-containing complex binding (Figure 4; Figures S3-S6). Similar to previous analyses, there was limited overlap between sexes among top IPA canonical pathways, but substantial overlap between diseases and disorders associated with gene expression differences. Htt and Fmr1 were shared upstream regulators identified across male and female mice. Follow-up analysis of Fmr1 sequence in C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice found mainly intronic variants (Table S24). The qPCR analysis did not support a clear difference in Fmr1 expression between alcohol and learning groups (p > 0.05), supporting the importance of the broader Fmr1-associated network in determining alcohol and learning phenotypes (Figure S2).
DISCUSSION

We assessed strain differences in dorsal hippocampal gene expression patterns associated with fear conditioning, alcohol exposure, and their interaction. Major differences in gene expression were observed between strains. Notably, in alcohol and fear conditioning naive DBA/2J males, we observed lower levels of Chrna7 transcript than condition-matched C57BL/6J males. A prior study from our laboratory using males and females found that DBA/2J mice were less sensitive to the disruptive effects of alcohol than C57BL/6J mice. These results are in line with a previous study that found reduced alcohol-induced contextual learning deficits in Chrna7 knockout mice. Alcohol also disrupted transcript levels differentially across strains and sex. Some notable pathways associated with alcohol's actions were GDNF (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor) family ligand-receptor interactions in female C57BL/6J mice and PKA (Protein Kinase A) in male DBA/2J mice. Further, it is possible that strain differences in alcohol-associated deficits in contextual fear learning were related to upstream regulator Fmr1, identified in both male and female analyses. Thus, alcohol may disrupt learning via interactions with pathways associated with Chrna7, GDNF, PKA, and Fmr1, which could be points of intervention for future studies.
Impact of strain, learning, or alcohol on gene expression

The main goals of this study were (1) To identify alcohol-disrupted learning-related gene expression in adolescents and (2) To understand why adolescent C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice differed in contextual learning outcomes after alcohol exposure. We predicted that complex interactions between strain, alcohol treatment, and fear learning exposure contributed to observed fear learning outcomes described in prior research. However, before examining possible interactions among factors, we examined the impact of each factor individually (strain, learning, and alcohol) on the dorsal hippocampal transcriptome.

Among the three factors (strain, drug, and fear learning) that were examined, strain differences were, predictably, the most pronounced. In males and females, 3526 and 2675 transcripts, respectively, were differentially regulated between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains (FDR <0.05). These transcriptional changes were an order of magnitude greater than those seen due to alcohol or fear conditioning exposures alone, as alcohol exposure resulted in 114-142 differentially regulated transcripts and fear conditioning led to 128-279 differentially regulated transcripts within strain and sex groups. These gene expression differences likely correspond to known strain differences in fear conditioning phenotypes.

An exciting observation from pairwise comparisons across strains was that in male subjects, Chrna7 transcript levels were lower in DBA/2J subjects than in C57BL/6J subjects in saline no-learning control subjects. This was not the case in female subjects. Prior research established that Chrna7 knockout male and female mice are less susceptible to alcohol effects on contextual fear learning. Thus, it is intriguing that DBA/2J males have lower Chrna7 transcript levels and are less susceptible to alcohol effects on contextual fear learning that C57BL/6J males. This could suggest an important role for Chrna7 and its protein product, the alpha7 subunit of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, in shaping susceptibility to alcohol's cognitive effects. Specifically, having lower Chrna7 expression, and possibly fewer alpha7 subunit-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, may predispose DBA/2J subjects to being less affected by alcohol in this learning task. Studies examining alpha7 subunits have shown unique roles for this subunit in modulating other alcohol phenotypes. For example, deletion of the alpha7 subunit (in null mutant male and female mice) produced exaggerated locomotor stimulation, sedation (LORR duration), and hypothermia phenotypes after alcohol exposure. alpha7 knockout female mice have also been shown to consume smaller amounts of alcohol. Our data fit into a broader narrative implicating alcohol effects on the cholinergic system as being critical for short- and long-term effects of adolescent alcohol exposure on learning and memory. However, our data suggest that this may not apply to female subjects, warranting more detailed follow-up studies in females. Chrna7 would also be an intriguing target to examine further in humans, as it is expressed throughout the nervous system and variation in this gene has been associated with other cognitive and drug-associated conditions, including nicotine dependence.
Disruption of learning-related gene expression by alcohol

Relative to observed transcriptional differences between strains, there were far fewer alcohol-associated transcriptional changes (176-190 differentially regulated transcripts). Prior studies have demonstrated that acute alcohol exposure often leads to transcriptional changes in the hippocampus associated with neuroplasticity. Because learning and memory relies on this plasticity, we suspected that alcohol might disrupt contextual fear learning by inhibiting neuroplasticity in the dorsal hippocampus. Comparisons between saline- and alcohol-treated subjects that had undergone fear conditioning showed some support for this. For example, among female C57BL/6J mice, a top canonical pathway was GDNF (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor) family ligand-receptor interactions; GDNF is thought to contribute to neuroplasticity and, consequently, learning and memory. However, top canonical pathways did not consistently include GDNF across both strains and sexes examined. This further indicates that genetic mechanisms underlying learning after alcohol exposure differ due to strain and sex.

Another notable finding was that Protein Kinase A (PKA) was a top canonical pathway associated with alcohol exposure among fear conditioned male DBA/2J subjects. It has also been shown that PKA is important in learning and memory. Ablation of some PKA isoforms has been shown to disrupt hippocampal long-term potentiation in male and female mice, and inhibiting PKA activity impaired contextual and cued fear conditioning in male rats. Furthermore, male rats treated with a low dose of alcohol shifted learning strategies from a hippocampus-based strategy to a striatal-based strategy, which suggests that alcohol changed how learning occurred. This shift in strategy was associated with decreased PKA activation. Thus, it is possible that alcohol regulates learning performance in DBA/2J males by dysregulating PKA signaling.
Strain differences in disruption of learning-related gene expression by alcohol

To assess why in prior work C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains exhibited differences in contextual fear learning after alcohol exposure, dorsal hippocampal gene expression was compared across strains among subjects that had undergone alcohol and fear conditioning exposures. The number of transcript-level differences between groups was relatively high (2816-3847 differentially regulated transcripts), largely due to the drastic differences observed between strains independent of drug or fear conditioning exposures. The canonical pathways and diseases and disorders associated with these strain differences were variable across males and females, with some canonical pathways related to immune signaling seen in both males and females (Activation of IRF by Cytosolic Pattern Recognition Receptors, IL-3 Signaling).

While sex differences in the RNA-sequencing data were generally pronounced, there was some noteworthy convergence in upstream regulators associated with transcriptional differences across sexes in this analysis. In both males and females, transcript differences between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J mice that were treated with alcohol and fear conditioned were associated with upstream regulators, Htt (huntingtin) and Fmr1 (fragile X mental retardation syndrome 1). Htt, while associated with many differentially regulated transcripts, was not differentially expressed between strains in males or females. However, Fmr1 transcript levels were significantly greater in DBA/2J mice than in C57BL/6J in male and female comparisons, making it a desirable candidate for future investigation. Fmr1 encodes fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP), which is likely an RNA-binding protein. As its name suggests, it has been associated with fragile X syndrome and autism-like phenotypes. Male and female Fmr1 knockout mice display numerous behavioral deficits depending on their strain background, including abnormal anxiety-like behaviors and social behaviors  and impairments in learning tasks, including contextual fear conditioning. Further, in Drosophila, FMRP dysregulation has been associated with alterations in PKA activity, noted in a previous section for being dysregulated in alcohol-treated fear conditioned subjects. PKA and FMRP interact in a negative feedback loop, suggesting that higher FMRP levels could be related to low PKA levels. This could contribute to learning deficits. Thus, it is possible that altered expression of Fmr1 due to alcohol and fear conditioning leads to dysregulation of Fmr1-associated networks, and this may drive observed fear learning differences after alcohol between C57BL/6J and DBA/2J strains. Importantly, the SNP analysis of Fmr1 did not indicate likely functional variants between strains, supporting that strain differences are likely the consequence of differential expression of Fmr1 rather than functional changes within the gene.

passages.text: Limitations and future directions

RNA-sequencing enabled a discovery-based approach to examining alcohol- and learning-associated transcriptional patterns. Interpretation of these data was informed by existing literature examining mechanisms of alcohol's behavioral effects. While it would have been informative to include numerous strains in the RNA-sequencing experiments, using two strains, C57BL/6J and DBA/2J, allowed for inclusion of more groups to examine separate alcohol and learning influences. We also chose to examine one time point in the gene expression study. Prior studies provide robust support for the value of this timepoint in assessing gene expression changes associated with fear learning in adult C57BL6/CBAF1 and C57BL/6J mice. Candidate genes identified by RNA-sequencing in our study may later be investigated using RT-qPCR in other strains, in adult subjects, or at different timepoints after learning or alcohol treatment. This may also be examined in future studies in specific cell types, as our study examined general differences across dorsal hippocampal tissue.

Further, strain differences in brain regions other than the dorsal hippocampus may have contributed to observed variation in fear learning after alcohol exposure. We chose to focus on the dorsal hippocampus because of the known role of the dorsal hippocampus in spatial learning, alcohol's known effects on the hippocampus  and the role of the hippocampus in numerous alcohol-related pathologies, such as Major Depressive Disorder . The ventral hippocampus, while important for fear learning, plays a broader role in fear association and expression. Because alcohol had greater effects on contextual fear conditioning when compared to cued fear conditioning, we focused on a brain region that contributes more specifically to contextual fear conditioning. While it is outside the scope of the proposed research, the roles of other brain regions, such as the ventral hippocampus and amygdala, in contextual learning deficits could be investigated in future studies. Future researchers will be able to compare their findings to ours, which are publicly available.

It is important to note that alcohol-associated gene expression was evaluated in fear conditioned subjects from both strains and sexes, but results of IPA analysis revealed little convergence across strain and sex groups in the functional enrichment of those transcriptional changes. This suggests it is likely that alcohol disrupts learning through unique mechanisms across the sexes and genetic backgrounds.
CONCLUSION

Understanding the biological basis of alcohol sensitivity is critical for understanding and preventing the development of AUD. Here, we describe how individual differences such as genetic background and sex shape susceptibility to alcohol's effects during adolescence and shape differences in hippocampus-dependent learning. We found robust differences in dorsal hippocampal gene expression between strains and sexes. Alcohol and learning both altered gene expression and produced unique transcriptional patterns across groups. Thus, differences in hippocampal gene expression biological networks were seen across strains, sex, and alcohol exposure. This suggests that mechanisms of learning are not homogenous but are influenced by genetics, sex, and drug exposure, which could result in differences in learning strategies and outcomes. Within this dataset, we identified biological pathways that could be involved in alcohol's effects on learning and memory, such as those associated with Chrna7 or Fmr1. Future research can followup on targets identified in this project to better understand how to modulate and possibly prevent alcohol-associated contextual learning impairments.
